What Is Account-Based Marketing? A Small-Team Version

By lowob · 27 May 2026 · Updated 10 November 2026 · 4-minute read · Revenue / B2B

A small B2B company doesn't always need thousands of leads. If ten customers could meaningfully change its revenue, it may make more sense to identify those customers and work deliberately to earn their business.

That is account-based marketing, or ABM: sales and marketing focus on a named set of companies that fit the product, rather than trying to reach everyone and hoping the right buyers respond.

What account-based marketing actually means

Start with a shortlist of companies whose problems the product can solve. Learn who is involved in the buying decision, why the timing may be right and what would make the company willing to talk. Use that knowledge to make outreach, content and follow-up relevant.

This is not just a mass email sequence with someone's first name inserted. It is a coordinated way of deciding where limited sales and marketing effort should go.

LinkedIn's ABM guide outlines three broad stages: account research, creating relevant content, and executing and measuring campaigns. A small team can do those jobs with ordinary research tools and a CRM rather than a large enterprise software package.

Use ABM when the customer is worth knowing individually

ABM is a natural fit when a sale has meaningful value, takes time and involves several stakeholders. Think of a fintech infrastructure provider selling to banks, an enterprise AI company selling into a regulated workflow, or a Web3 service courting funds and custodians.

It's less suitable when the product is cheap, self-serve and bought spontaneously, or when the team cannot identify buyers before they arrive. In those cases, broad product-led acquisition or simpler inbound channels may work better.

The key question is whether knowing and contacting a particular company is worth the work involved.

Build a short list you can actually work

For a hypothetical fintech infrastructure startup, a sensible starting list might be 20 to 50 potential accounts, not an arbitrarily large database. The right size depends on deal value and team capacity.

For each account, record the business fit, a relevant recent signal, likely buyer roles and a plausible reason to talk. A company launching a new payment product, hiring for treasury operations or expanding internationally may have a specific need. Verify the signal instead of inventing a problem based on the job title.

Account

A company with a problem the product demonstrably solves.

Reason to talk

A relevant change, public statement, introduction or evidence of unmet need.

Next step

One specific person, one credible message and a clear follow-up owner.

Assign an owner to each account so marketing and sales aren't contacting the same people with conflicting messages.

Run a small program before buying a large platform

Prepare a short research note for each account. Write a message based on the business problem, not biographical trivia. Support it with useful material such as a relevant product explanation, technical documentation or a properly evidenced case study.

Use partner introductions, thoughtful email and professional communities where relevant. An event or small roundtable can help with conversations that take multiple stakeholders. Coordinate follow-ups in a shared CRM.

Review the list every two weeks. Ask which accounts have progressed, what objections came up and whether the target list still makes sense. The original article suggested 50 accounts and a recurring review; those are workable examples, not universal requirements.

Measure progress by account, not by email volume

Track meetings with relevant decision-makers, new stakeholders engaged, technical or commercial diligence completed, qualified opportunities and eventual sales. A hundred opens are not a substitute for one serious buyer conversation.

Include the team's research and follow-up effort in the economics. ABM can create a compelling sales process, but it is not automatically cheaper than other channels. It works when the value of winning a fitting account justifies the time invested.

lowob takeaways

  • Start with identifiable high-fit buyers. A short list can be more useful than a large lead funnel.
  • Research the business need. Personalize the reason to talk, not just the greeting.
  • Coordinate sales and marketing. Give each account one owner and one coherent approach.
  • Measure account movement. Meetings, diligence, opportunities and customers matter more than outreach volume.

Sources and notes

LinkedIn Marketing Solutions, Understanding Account-Based Marketing. Background framework for research, tailored content, execution and measurement.

The fintech startup and suggested list size are illustrative. The specific scale of an ABM program should follow the sales cycle, buyer value and available team capacity.
